CHINA AIRWAYS FEDERAL INC. U.S. A.
3 CANTON ROAD
SHANGHAI
NORTH AMERICAN AVIATION, INC.
INTERCONTINENT AVIATION, INC.
CURTISS WRIGHT CORPORATION
CURTISS AEROPLANE AND MOTOR COMPANY
WRIGHT AERONAUTICAL CORPORATION
CURTISS- WRIGHT AIRPLANE COMPANY
DOUGLAS AIRCRAFT COMPANY
SPERRY GYROSCOPE COMPANY
HANKOW, Saturday, June 3, 1933.
Dear
We arrived here yesterday afternoon at
5 P.M. after a beautiful and most interesting trip down
from Chungking through the gorges. We flew low in a regular
Loening with landing wheels removed - in other words a flying
The pilot who has been flying this 500-mile-route for
neariy two years 1s a great character. He is from Nashv11le
and knows the Holdneress and others from there. He is very
good looking - a big fellow about 5:l1 and weighs 180 or
thereabouts - his drawl is not very pronounced but you would
know he hails from the South. His name is Charles S. Vaughn
but he is known on every steamboat, gunboat, city and town -
by all nationalities including Chinese as "Chilly". All up
and down the upper Yangtze for the 500 miles the expression
"Here comes Chilly" is a part of the every day language and
among the Chinese "Here comes Chilly" means aviation or air
ma. i1.
He has & Ilat in Hankow where lots of passenger and
all the pilots make their headquarters. He charges the
pilots on the lower river run $6.00 Mex. per day and they
sign
"chits" for drinks or extras. (Any memo, short note or
club slip over here is a "chit") He has a good Chinese boy
as cook and another as servant - press suits, shine shoes, etc.
When Chilly goes along the river all the boats whistle a
salute and Chilly flashes the most engaging smile you've ever
seen and waves to crew and passengers as he roars by. He has
a stop at Ichang where
the gorges begin and there is stationed
the American "flag-pan" as the naval officers call the flag
ship of the Yangtsze River flat bottomed gun boats. When we
landed for gas at Ichang near the "flag-pan" the admiral
called out "come on over Chilly" so we got in a sampan and
jointed the officers on the Luzon, which is the "flag-pans"
official name, and had a cup of coffee and a sandwich while
Chilly's Chinese co-pilot Hugh Chen was supervising the
refueling of-the ship.
I noticed as we approached the flag
ship that all the sailors and even the cook said "Hello Chilly".
If he gets stuck at Ichang, Chilly boards the Luzon with any
foreign passengers he may have and spends the night on board
flying on the next morning to Chungking. In two years he has
never had an accident of any kind and he is so well known
that his plane is filled to capacity on almost every trip.
writes notes to the foreign passengers and Chen writes notes
to the Chinese passengers pointing out interesting places, etc.
At Chungking Chilly had a flat but every time he arrived there
different people insisted on entertaining him and so he gave
up his flat and for two years has stayed with friends up there.

- 2-
Well so much for Chilly - you may meet him
because he is going home on leave in August and maybe to get
married although he claims his girl is still saying "no"
instead of "yas". He has been over here 3 years and all
pilots get 3 months home with expenses and full pay every
3 years.
He says he wants to be back here by Xmas.
Well to return to our flight.
We left Chungking
at 9 A.M. and flew East through beautiful country very much
like Lake George except the broad Yangtze is coffee color
rather than blue.
China is much more enjoyable from the air
than from the surface because you see only the beautiful
green country and you miss all
the squallor, dirt and most
unpleasant of all, the odors. Someone was asked if he knew
the Chinese National Anthem. He replied that at no place
had he ever heard the National air but that he could smell it
almost anywhere.
Our first landing was at Wahnsien which is
a quaint city at the upper end of the gorges.
From there we
flew close to the river through the gorges which rise steep
on either side from 500 to 1500 feet.
There we flew for a
hundred miles about 30 feet off the water. (It is now Sunday
morning and again I am flying down the Yangtze with Shanghai
as our last stop.
We have just left Chekiang where the ship
which we were supposed to take back to Shanghai yesterday
morning was forced down Friday afternoon by motor trouble.
pilot Howard Norris and mechanic "Swede" Larsen met us at the
float - the engine is in bad shape and the plane will have to
be loaded on to a river boat and shipped back to Shanghai. The
pilot and mechanic will stay with the ship until it is loaded.
I asked Norris to buy me some Chekiang china which is quite
famous and I think very beautiful - it is called "thousand
flowers" and I wrote to you about it once before. The flowers
are all different colors against & blueish gold back ground or
a black back ground.
I ordered the lighter back ground and
will send one of the plates to you for your approval or
disapproval. If the latter, I can easily dispose of them in
Shanghai at
more than Norris will pay for them.
He thought he
could get & fairly good set of six pieces each for $60.00 Mex.
or $15.00 our money. To go on with my story of the gorges.-
we passed many picturesque junks with their delapidated sails,
miscelaneous cargos struggling up stream against the swift
current and white capped rapids of the muddy snarling Yangtsze.
A rope is attached to the mast of the junk - a long long bamboo
twisted rope - trackers frequently stark naked strain with all
their strength, their bare feet gripping the tow path worn
smoothe by generations of their sweating chanting grunting
ancestors who for thousands of years have fought up stream along
the same path towing the
same type of cargo in the same kind
of junks. The latter vary in design so that experienced
observers can tell at a glance where the junk is from.
of them will travel from Shanghai to the borders of Tibet.
places along the cliffs the tracker path is hewn out of solid
rock and the trackers, from six to ten men depending on the
size of the tow,
cling to the narrow path with rock above their
heads - one shoulder rubbing the cliff and the other above a
yawning chasm 100 feet above the river where a slip means just

-3-
one more Chinese ancestor.
"Chilly" comes down lower still
and passes close to a river steam boat which appears to be
standing still but is actually running with every horse in its
horsepower pulling his darndest against the swift current. Crew
and passengers wave as we flash by - just caught a glimpse of
the flag, it was British.
We
take the bends of the river with
a gentle
banking turn - the air is smoothe - it should be
rough - our two Chinese companions - a man and his wife are
both asleep, apparently old customers of Chilly's. Along the
steep sides of the gorges wherever any soil is available
terraced rice fields get a rest while the farmer coolies watch
us pass - they never change expressions or wave. Little shrines
are carved out of the rock at many places and ocassionally you
see a small pagoda.
Emerging from the gorges we land at Ichang -
the break bulk station and transhipment point between the upper
and lower Yangtsze. Ichang is known for canes which are carved
out of a tree root. I had radioed our agent to have some there
for me to look at and bought three for $1.00 Mex. each. (We have
1 900 но%.
just landed to deliver and take on mail at Anking - our station
there is a raft like pontoon and attached to it is half & junk
in which is a waiting room.
We stayed there a few minutes and
then take off for Nanking.
We fly over the ancient city of
Anking•
It is entirely surrounded by a high wall with & moat.
One gate - is the only entrance on the river side and one on
the land side. We have one Chinese passenger who wakes up only
to get out at each station and take a smoke. He has on a long
blue gown and a skull cap like Guido Pantaleoni wears) We
arrived at Hankow Friday afternoon - it was quite hot 88° in
the shade and my winter suit was uncomfortable. Chilly's boy
pressed it for me which at least made it look more presentable.
We had dinner at Chilly's and then went to a movie "Tomorrow
and Tomorrow".
I had seen it before but didn't say so because
they all wanted to go and it was the only movie in town. Satur-
day A.M. we saw Chilly off for Chungking again and went shopping.
I bought some "shorts" with stockings to match - olive drab -
and felt much more comfortable - also felt (but wasn't) more
conspicuous • We had lunch at Chilly's place and as it was
raining just sat around until the plane, in which I am now
writing, came in at 3 o'clock.
went out to the club
and had
a swim after which we drank tea on the porch - watched
a cricket game "just îwancy" and listened to a band, or rather
orchestra, play some very good music which wound up with "God
Save the King" amid much bumping of glasses and toasts - it was
the king's birthday - quite an event it seems among the English
who seem to control the Hankow Club as well as every other
club in China except the American and French Clubs at Shanghai.
The cricket game was the first I have ever seen and I found
it much less boring than I expected - probably because one
American was playing and refused to make futile passes at the
ball but instead took a full man-sized baseball swing and
knocked the ball out of the lot every time the "bowler" threw
the ball toward his wicket. After the American had scored
45 runs the game was stopped for some reason - probably for tea
or perhaps they despaired of ever getting him out. However all
the Britishers gave him a great hand and didn't seem to resent

-4-
his breaking up the game. He also was very modest and
un-American in the sense of the all too customary swash
buckling braggart type. As a matter of fact the Chinese
classify all white men as
"foreigners" and there is a
resultant spirit of comradie which is quite refreshing and
@iten you entirely forget whether your companion is English,
French or what have you.
We are now approaching Nanking the present
Capital of China. Except for the immediate section around
about here and the recognition by foreign governments Nanking
is a Capital in name only. The far away provinces pledge
allegiance to the National Government but they pay in practically
no taxes and the various generals (or bandits - until they win)
fight it out for control.
They give nothing to, nor do they
receive anything from, the National Treasury at Nanking so I
guess its about the same as the U.S. in the last analysis -
except the people of China do not have to put up with & Senate
and Congress and you must admit that is one blessing which goes
far to make up for many hardships. Over here a man in public
life can eat Swifts bacon without any danger of impeachment for
favoring big business.
When I read of the actions of the U.S.
Senate I can not help but admire the Chinese system.
Here at
least a leader of men must be a real man among his fellows - he
must possess & keen quick mind and a two fisted virility.
Oh
well anyhow Nanking. Leaving Nanking we have another passenger
who we learn from the station manager is Mr. Chen, Police
Commissioner of Hankow, formerly Police Commissioner at Shanghai.
I'm told he lost his job at Shanghai because he caught the
Mayor smuggling opium at which job it seems the Mayor had been
working for
several years quite
to the advantage of said Mayor's
bank account. Mr. Mayor was given someother job and the Police
Commissioner was told to be less zealous.
I guess they were
afraid he might get "too high up on the hog" as brother Bill says.
Holl one - Our first Chinese passenger just got a
little touch of air sickness.
As Gent Shelton said of Speed
Elliot - "he is two shades whiter than a swan".
Must quit now.
We're approaching Shanghai and
I must pack up and really go back to hard work after this
inspection trip.
Lots and lots of love-
Big
Found six lettus hers
and the
from you from yet girls
guelo -
one Each from the guls.

Bixby to his wife, Debby Bixby, dated Saturday, June 3, 1933 from Hankow, on stationery from China Airways Federal Inc.; includes description of Charles S. “Chilly” [Chili] Vaughn and their flight from Chungking [Chongqing] to Hankow [Hankou] and Nanking [Nanjing]; mentions Hugh Chen.
